metadata.title: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock rebounds as spy fiasco involving CEO Jensen Huang raises broader risk concerns

content.text:
Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock rebounds as spy fiasco involving CEO Jensen Huang raises broader risk concerns
Nvidia (NVDA) stock rebounded on Wednesday as the overall chip sector surged on the heels of CoreWeave's (CRWV) better-than-expected quarterly results.
Nvidia shares rose for the first time since CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, rising roughly 5% after two straight days of declines. The company's board has launched an investigation into the affair.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang wrote in a memo to employees.
The Information reported on Tuesday that Alice Huang is believed to be involved in a network of Chinese companies that facilitated the shipment of $7.5 billion in chip sales to China.
Given the size and importance of Nvidia in the stock market today, the revelation marks one of the biggest CEO-personal conduct scandals in history. It also highlights Nvidia's key-person risk and uncertain succession plan as questions swirl about whether the board will ask Huang to step down.
The news has drawn immediate and varied reactions from leaders ranging from the US president to other CEOs. President Trump stood by Huang, calling him "an honorable guy," but other members of the president's party are expected to put more scrutiny on the company.
Trump also stated on Monday that the FBI was looking into Huang's relationship.
In a statement on Sunday, Nvidia's board said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised."
Follow along for live updates and reactions.
- Brian Sozzi
'Icarus' rise and fall': Analyst downgrades Nvidia stock amid Jensen Huang woes, highlights risks
Let Wall Street analyst downgrades begin on the once-untouchable Nvidia (NVDA) stock in the wake of CEO Jensen Huang's high-profile affair.
Baird analyst Tristan Gerra cut his rating on Nvidia to Neutral on Wednesday in a note titled "Icarus' Rise and Fall; Company Will Be Fine."
"Downgrading to Neutral until uncertainties regarding U.S. government action likely resulting from the upcoming congressional hearing are lifted, U.S. government investigations reach their conclusions, revenue impact from risk channel near-term adjustments along with potential charges is quantified, and uncertainties around CEO tenure clear," Gerra wrote. Read more.
- Grace O'Donnell
Rep. Mast prepared to subpoena Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: ABC News
Rep. Brian Mast, the Republican chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee from Florida, told ABC News on Tuesday that he's prepared to issue a subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over Huang's affair that's believed to have involved a Chinese spy.
Republicans, including Mast, Select China Committee chair Rep. John Moolenaar, and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence chair Rep. Rick Crawford, sent a letter to Huang, requesting that he attend a closed-door briefing on his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is believed to work for China's government intelligence service.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the letter stated. "The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk."
Jensen Huang has until Nov. 11 to respond and set a date for the closed hearing. If Huang doesn't respond, Mast said he could be subpoenaed.
- Ines Ferré
Trump told about Chinese spying on Nvidia CEO by Marco Rubio in May, en route to China: Report
President Trump was reportedly told aboard Air Force One in May that US intelligence showed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, according to a New York Times report published on Tuesday afternoon.
The outlet, citing people familiar with the matter, said Secretary of State and national security adviser Marco Rubio delivered the warning shortly before Huang joined Trump's trip to Beijing. Huang joined the trip to China with other tech titans, at the last minute at Mr. Trump's invitation.
The report marks at least the second time in seven months that Trump was briefed on intelligence concerning Huang and the woman.
- Ines Ferré
Nvidia stock extends losses, sinks 6%
Nvidia (NVDA) stock hovered near session lows, dropping more than 6% after falling 4% in the prior session. The stock came under pressure amid a broader market sell-off and growing concerns about increased scrutiny of the chipmaker following CEO Jensen Huang's admission to an affair believed to involve a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Scrutiny centers on Alice Huang, whom the US government reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset, and her ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dating back to at least 2023
According to two people who know her and corporate records reported by The Information, their rapport helped facilitate the shipment of at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Chinese companies.
172.83 +4.03 (+2.39%)As of 10:00:26 AM EST. Market Open. - Yahoo Finance
AI chip exports to China and oversight bills gain momentum in Congress
Yahoo Finance breaks down several bills before Congress to limit AI chips.
Why analysts aren't trying to ruffle Nvidia's feathers amid CEO scandal
Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi weighs in on why analysts are largely silent on Nvidia amid CEO scandal.
- Grace O'Donnell
Nvidia CEO's affair enabled $7.5 billion in chip sales to China: Information
The Information reported on Tuesday that Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with alleged spy Alice Huang dates back to 2023 and enabled Chinese companies to acquire $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips.
According to the report, Alice Huang, her sister, and her husband built a web of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips. One of those companies at the center of the network is Shanghai Century Litong, a company based in China that was added to Nvidia's list of preferred cloud partners.
When the US banned the export of Nvidia's most powerful chips to China, Alice Huang helped secure 240,000 chips from distributors in China, including H100, H200, and A100 chips, according to the report.
Century Litong said the company obtained Nvidia's preferred cloud partner qualification through compliant channels.
"All business resources of our company are obtained in compliance with applicable laws and regulations," the company told The Information. "Our company has no business dealings with Ms. Huang."
- Jared Blikre
Jensen Huang's spy scandal may cost Nvidia the China chip fight it was winning
Jensen Huang was Washington's loudest voice against cutting China off from American chips, and his spy scandal is now the hawks' best argument. Meanwhile, the Commerce Department hasn't added a single company to its export ban list in 13 months.
The Nvidia (NVDA) CEO admitted Sunday to an affair with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials believe worked for China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia stock fell about 4% Monday, even as chip stocks (^SOX) jumped nearly 7%. That was Nvidia's worst day during a 5%-plus chip rally since Oct. 28, 1999, months after it went public.
The list in question is Commerce's Entity List. Companies on it need a US license to buy American technology, and those licenses are rarely granted. Commerce added 170 names in 2025 and 366 the year before. It hasn't added one since Oct. 9, 2025, by Yahoo Finance's count.
On Monday, Commerce extended its pause on a rule that would stretch those limits to companies majority-owned by listed firms. But only by two months, to Jan. 10, a week after a new Democratic Congress is sworn in.
"I think Commerce Department is going to batten down the hatches, and they're going to enforce export controls in a way that they weren't doing it before," Isaac Stone Fish, CEO and founder of Strategy Risks, told Deirdre Bosa on Monday.
- Grace O'Donnell
Nvidia is worth nearly 30% less if Jensen Huang is no longer CEO: Tech analyst
Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi reports:
A big valuation haircut could be coming to what was once the world's most valuable company by market cap, Nvidia (NVDA), if newly embattled CEO Jensen Huang is forced to leave.
"We believe if Jensen was removed as CEO, Nvidia is worth a lot less (25%-30%) as a company/stock and would change the future direction of the company and create a dramatically different competitive environment around AI GPUs both in the US and globally especially for China," Yorkville Ives partner and veteran tech analyst Dan Ives said on Tuesday.
Nvidia stock fell 4.27% on Monday as a dark cloud settled over Nvidia and its once-Teflon CEO's future. Shares fell slightly in pre-market trading on Tuesday.
Added Ives, "Jensen is the core DNA of Nvidia and its AI success and ambitions are heavily tied to him staying on as CEO. Jensen is not replaceable..there is no other person on the management team bench that can step in seamlessly as CEO and that speaks to the key man risk now with Nvidia that investors will factor this dynamic to the stock."
- Grace O'Donnell
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair appears to have short-circuited Wall Street analysts
Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi reports:
If the Wall Street analysts who power consensus estimates are concerned about Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang's shocking affair with an alleged Chinese spy, they sure aren't showing it.
In its earnings preview on Nvidia (NVDA) released Monday at 5 a.m. ET, Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider didn't mention the issue once, even though it erupted over the weekend.
Citi analyst Atif Malik offered no opinion on the matter in a note out Tuesday, beyond outlining what investors are thinking.
"For investors, key issues are likely potential governance implications, increased regulatory scrutiny and export-control compliance of the flow of H200 chips into China (<1% of DC sales) and routed through other intermediaries, and longer-term impact on leadership stability. The company has stated that Mr. Huang will remain CEO while the investigation proceeds," Malik said.
Other top investment banks, such as JPMorgan, Evercore ISI and Jefferies, haven't published anything on Nvidia since the scandal broke. Nvidia lists 47 analysts covering the company.
"It's bizarre," one former sell-side analyst told me.
- Ines Ferré
Trump says FBI 'looking into' Nvidia CEO scandal
President Trump on Monday told reporters the FBI is "looking into" Nvidia's (NVDA) Jensen Huang after the CEO of the AI chip giant admitted having an affair with a woman whom US intelligence reportedly believes was likely gathering information for Beijing.
Trump told reporters at the White House that he was made aware of the matter "not too long ago."
"We'll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else," Trump said.
- Brian Sozzi
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a reported Chinese spy damages this key investing factor
Investing in a public company's stock is more than crunching numbers.
I have heard from a lot of you about the hot water that Nvidia's (NVDA) celebrated CEO, Jensen Huang, is in following his admission to having cheated on his wife of 40-plus years with a reported Chinese spy. I said on X (see below) that Nvidia is now in its first true crisis, arguably since its founding in 1993.
Some of you pushed back on me for coining it a crisis, calling attention to Nvidia's strong demand pipeline and leadership position in AI chips. I suspect Jensen's vision has helped make you a lot of money through the years, so I get why the first instinct is to sweep this under the rug and voice support for Huang.
I am not going to deny that you have a point on the fundamentals of the business. I also won't deny that Huang is a generational founder of a transformational business.
But make no mistake: This is a crisis created by Huang that didn't need to happen. And it all boils down to trust. Read more.
- Ines Ferré
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries signals congressional oversight of Nvidia
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Monday that Congress "will need a full briefing" and that there are "real concerns to address" regarding AI chip maker Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair believed to be with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Jeffries added that lawmakers need more information.
A briefing typically marks an initial procedural step before formal hearings are scheduled.
172.83 +4.03 (+2.39%)As of 10:00:26 AM EST. Market Open. - Brian Sozzi
Nvidia has a 'deep bench' if Jensen Huang steps aside, tech investor says
Nvidia can still crush it in the coming years if embattled CEO Jensen Huang is forced to step away from the company.
When asked how important Huang is to the next few years of the AI chip darling, Niles Investment Management founder and longtime tech investor Dan Niles told Sozzi Unleashed that he "isn't."
"[Huang's] got a very deep bench, and a historical example is what happened to Apple after Steve Jobs passed away. … Did it collapse?" Niles said. "So Jensen's done a great job of empowering people underneath him. I think one thing that will happen is there will be a successor appointed. The board will force that. And so I think that will occur out of this."
"Are the products in the pipeline, much like when Steve Jobs passed away, that will keep the company going for the next couple of years? Absolutely," Niles added. "But is Jensen very important to the company? Completely. So those are two separate thoughts. But they can both coexist."
- Ines Ferré
Singapore-based company at center of Nvidia CEO scandal pushes back against claims of diverting banned chips to China
The Singapore-based AI infrastructure company at the center of the scrutiny after Nvidia's (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang's affair has pushed back against claims that it illegally diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed said on LinkedIn it had undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews over the preceding six months by the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, and Nvidia. According to the company, the reviews found no evidence of illicit chip transfers or other illegal activities. The statement, which references a Bloomberg article, was posted on its website featuring a December 2025 date.
The pushback follows reports about Huang's relationship with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who has reportedly been investigated over suspected links to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Sunday, though he did not name the woman with whom he had an affair.
Months before Huang's admitted affair and the board investigation into the matter made headlines, activist short seller Culper Research raised concerns over the world's leading AI chipmaker's exposure to China.
The report specifically flagged Megaspeed, which the short seller claimed had underlying financial ties to Chinese tech giant Alibaba. The researchers also pointed to Jenson Huang's relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.
- Ines Ferré
US Commerce Dept inquiry into Megaspeed halted after Nvidia intervened: Report
Nvidia (NVDA) reportedly contacted US Commerce Department investigators in August 2025 seeking information about a probe into Megaspeed, the Singapore-based AI infrastructure procurement company whose former executive, Alice Huang, has been linked to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
The New York Times reported on Monday that the investigation was subsequently transferred to the Justice Department after Commerce officials raised concerns about the contact. The DOJ is now conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed.
172.83 +4.03 (+2.39%)As of 10:00:26 AM EST. Market Open. - Daniel Howley
Analysts says Nvidia CEO unlikely to be ousted over affair, but raise questions about company's future
Wall Street analysts are reacting to news of Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy with a mixture of caution and concern about the company's future and what the episode means for the AI industry.
Moor Insights & Strategy CEO and chief analyst Patrick Moorhead told Yahoo Finance that he doesn't believe Huang will be pushed out unless the board's investigation turns up anything.
"The issue is that Jensen is the product strategist, the closer with the hyperscalers, and the face of the company in Washington and Beijing. This story puts that last role at risk," Moorehead said.
Wedbush analyst Matt Bryson wrote in a note to investors that the board's initial statement reduces the chances that it plans to oust Huang, but said doing so would be a significant negative for the company due to his "hands-on operating style."
But he wrote that the incident could hurt the CEO's credibility.
"Regardless of the outcome of the investigation, however, we necessarily see Jensen losing some of his power/credibility in advocating for AI and Nvidia with US government representatives (whether free trade with foreign entities or how the government regulates AI development)," Bryson wrote. Read more.
- Brian Sozzi
Nvidia's black eye: One company isn't run by one person
Yahoo Finance Executive Editor Brian Sozzi shares some of his thoughts on the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang's affair.
- Ines Ferré
Short seller warned of Nvidia's 'China problem' months before board investigation into CEO's admitted affair
Months before Nvidia's (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang's admitted affair and the board investigation into the matter made headlines, concerns over the world's leading AI chipmaker's exposure to China had already surfaced.
Back in May, activist short seller Culper Research said it initiated a short position in Nvidia, highlighting what it called 'The China Problem.' At the time, shares of the AI chip giant were trading near record highs. Culper stressed that its thesis was not a bet against enterprise AI adoption, but rather a warning that the market was significantly underpricing Nvidia's exposure to mainland China.
The short seller alleged that, even though Nvidia claimed its China sales had fallen to zero, upwards of 20% of the company's fiscal 2026 data-center and computing revenue remained tied to China via third-party diversion across Southeast Asia.
The report specifically flagged Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing provider and major Nvidia customer, which the short seller claimed had underlying financial ties to Chinese tech giant Alibaba. The researchers also flagged Huang's relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.
"Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has not only vouched for Megaspeed, but seems to have quite literally walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, while maintaining an uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang, a Chinese national," said the May report.
Pointing to rapid balance-sheet expansion at Megaspeed, the short seller questioned whether Nvidia was exercising enough diligence on the ultimate destination of its advanced chips. Megaspeed has denied participating in illegal hardware transfers, and Nvidia has maintained that its compliance audits found no evidence of export violations.
- Ines Ferré
SpaceX, Tesla's Elon Musk expresses support for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
SpaceX (SPCX) and Tesla (TSLA) CEO Elon Musk has publicly expressed support for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after he admitted to an extramarital affair and the company's board announced an independent investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
Musk wrote "I agree" when responding to a post on Sunday night written by Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital and prominent technology investor.
Macquire said, "Jensen is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation," and added, "he did something incredibly dumb," but added, "two mistakes don't make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership."
Wall Street sees congressional scrutiny ahead for Nvidia given national-security concerns stemming from reports that US intelligence officials believe the woman Huang was romantically involved with, Alice Huang, was working for Chinese intelligence.
Nvidia's board has said it has no reason to believe that national security or company secrets were compromised, but will investigate the matter.

Analysts says Nvidia CEO unlikely to be ousted over affair, but raise questions about company's future

Wall Street analysts are reacting to news of Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy with a mixture of caution and concern about the company's future and what the episode means for the AI industry.
Moor Insights & Strategy CEO and chief analyst Patrick Moorhead told Yahoo Finance that he doesn't believe Huang will be pushed out unless the board's investigation turns up anything.
"The issue is that Jensen is the product strategist, the closer with the hyperscalers, and the face of the company in Washington and Beijing. This story puts that last role at risk," Moorehead said.

Wedbush analyst Matt Bryson wrote in a note to investors that the board's initial statement reduces the chances that it plans to oust Huang, but said doing so would be a significant negative for the company due to his "hands-on operating style."
But he wrote that the incident could hurt the CEO's credibility.

"Regardless of the outcome of the investigation, however, we necessarily see Jensen losing some of his power/credibility in advocating for AI and Nvidia with US government representatives (whether free trade with foreign entities or how the government regulates AI development)," Bryson wrote. Short seller warned of Nvidia's 'China problem' months before board investigation into CEO's admitted affair

Months before Nvidia's (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang's admitted affair and the board investigation into the matter made headlines, concerns over the world's leading AI chipmaker's exposure to China had already surfaced.

Back in May, activist short seller Culper Research said it initiated a short position in Nvidia, highlighting what it called 'The China Problem.' At the time, shares of the AI chip giant were trading near record highs. Culper stressed that its thesis was not a bet against enterprise AI adoption, but rather a warning that the market was significantly underpricing Nvidia's exposure to mainland China.

The short seller alleged that, even though Nvidia claimed its China sales had fallen to zero, upwards of 20% of the company's fiscal 2026 data-center and computing revenue remained tied to China via third-party diversion across Southeast Asia.

The report specifically flagged Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing provider and major Nvidia customer, which the short seller claimed had underlying financial ties to Chinese tech giant Alibaba. The researchers also flagged Huang's relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.

"Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has not only vouched for Megaspeed, but seems to have quite literally walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, while maintaining an uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang, a Chinese national," said the May report.

Pointing to rapid balance-sheet expansion at Megaspeed, the short seller questioned whether Nvidia was exercising enough diligence on the ultimate destination of its advanced chips. Megaspeed has denied participating in illegal hardware transfers, and Nvidia has maintained that its compliance audits found no evidence of export violations.
